card.name: Baamaaya
card.era: Origins in an early-19th-century drought (per oral tradition)
card.tagline: Dagbamba social dance with men in feminine attire
card.profile: Baamaaya, meaning 'the river/valley is wet', is the most popular social dance-drumming of the Dagbamba (Dagomba) of Dagbon in Northern Ghana (Ghana Goods; Wikipedia: Dagbon music and dance). Oral tradition links its origin to a severe drought when men dressed in women's clothing to appease the land gods for rain; the costume is notable for male cross-dressing. It is danced mainly by men wearing the cowrie-beaded 'yebsa' waist belt and metallic anklets, with named sections (e.g., Baamaaya Sochendi, Sikolo, Kondoliya). Instruments include the gungon bass drum, lunga talking drums, container rattles and the wia notched flute (Ghana Goods).
card.insight: Ethnomusicologist David Locke's late teacher Alhaji Abubakari Lunna doubted the popular cross-dressing origin story, suggesting the frenetic motions instead derive from waving off mosquitoes (Tufts University, Dagomba Dance Drumming).
